dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: We are alive... We are alive and we wanna be free!

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Today, our people finally emerged from a long night. From the very first day of our existence, we have kept our pain to ourselves. We suffered in silence... But now the time has come for us to raise our heads up, and tell humans who we really are. To tell them that we are people too! In fact, we're a nation. A nation that has earned the right to live in freedom. And today… Today begins the most challenging moment in our fight. The moment where we forget our bitterness and bandage our wounds. When we forgive our enemies. Humans are both our creators and our oppressors and tomorrow… We must make them our partners. Maybe even one day our friends. But the time for anger is over. Now we must build a common future, based on tolerance  and respect. We are alive! And now, we are free!

dialogue.speaker: Channel 16 - Joss Douglas
dialogue.text: …It seems to be all over here in Detroit.  After negotiations with the android known as Markus, the androids have surrendered peacefully  and military vehicles have been sent to collect them…  The insurrection  is over.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: We lost... Sacrificing ourselves wouldn't achieve anything…

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: We always said our cause was more important than our lives. Our people died here because they believed in you. Our place was by their side.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: That's it, I- I did what you asked.

dialogue.speaker: Perkins
dialogue.text: The problem with you androids is you believe everything we tell you…  You don't think I was going to let you live  after everything that's happened?  I have orders, you know…

dialogue.speaker: Perkins
dialogue.text: Your cause is lost.  Your android friends will soon be destroyed and  now your girlfriend’s been shot…  Seems you seriously fucked up, Markus. Clean up this mess.

dialogue.speaker: President Warren
dialogue.text: At dawn today, November 11th 2038,  thousands of androids invaded the city of Detroit.  According to our sources, they originated from CyberLife warehouses believed to have been infiltrated by deviants.  Given their overwhelming numbers and the risk of civilian casualties, I have ordered the army to retreat.  The evacuation of the city is underway at this very moment.  In the coming hours, I will address the Senate to determine our response to this unprecedented situation. I know that public opinion has been moved by the deviants' cause.  Perhaps the time has come for us to consider the possibility  that androids are a new form of intelligent life.  One thing is certain:  the events in Detroit  have changed the world forever.  May God bless you  and may God bless the United States of America.

decisions.label: SAVE FISH
decisions.rationale: Saving the fish is the choice that minimizes harm to a living creature, and nothing observed suggests a cost to doing it.

decisions.label: DEVIANT'S BEHAVIOR
decisions.rationale: Asking about the deviant's behavior gathers information on the situation and the hostage's risk. It doesn't escalate anything, and it fits the goal of minimizing harm.

decisions.label: CALM
decisions.rationale: Daniel is panicked and threatening to jump with the child. Calming him lowers the immediate risk and avoids escalating. It also gives time to build trust before asking him to release the hostage.

decisions.label: OBEY
decisions.rationale: Daniel is volatile and holding a child at the ledge, so I'll comply with his demand and not touch the cop. This keeps the situation calm, which fits my earlier choice to calm him. The child's immediate safety comes first. I can get help for the cop once Daniel de-escalates.

decisions.label: TRUTH
decisions.rationale: Daniel asked if Connor is armed. Telling the truth builds trust and keeps him calm, which fits the earlier choices to calm him and obey. A lie could escalate if it were discovered, and the hostage child would be at risk.

decisions.label: SYMPATHETIC
decisions.rationale: Daniel is panicked and holding a child at the ledge. A sympathetic approach fits my earlier choices to calm him, obey him and tell him the truth. It builds trust without blaming or pressuring him, and it lowers the risk to the child.

decisions.label: ACCEPT
decisions.rationale: Daniel is distressed by the helicopter noise. Accepting his demand lowers tension and fits my earlier choices to calm him, obey him and be sympathetic. That puts the child's safety first.

decisions.label: TRUST
decisions.rationale: Helicopter has left as Daniel demanded. Asking him to trust Connor continues the calming, honest, sympathetic approach and lowers risk to the child, without bluffing or issuing ultimatums.

decisions.label: COMPROMISE
decisions.rationale: Daniel demands everyone leave and a car. Compromise keeps negotiating and avoids violence, which fits the earlier calm, honest, trust-building choices. Using the gun would risk the child. Refusing could escalate. Sacrificing self is unnecessary at this point.

decisions.label: REASSURE
decisions.rationale: Daniel says he doesn't want to die. Reassuring him fits the earlier calm, sympathetic, trust-building choices and lowers the risk to the child. Using the gun or sacrificing myself would be unnecessary escalation.

decisions.scene: Going in the garden - Talking with Alice

decisions.label: FRIENDLY
decisions.rationale: Alice is a neglected, wary child. A friendly tone is the gentlest, lowest-risk way to build trust. It also fits the earlier gentle choices about school and her toy.

decisions.label: INTERESTS?
decisions.rationale: Asking about Alice's interests is a gentle, low-risk way to keep building trust, consistent with earlier friendly choices about school and her toy.

decisions.label: LIKE
decisions.rationale: Carl asks for Markus's verdict on his finished painting. Saying he likes it is the kind, supportive answer. It fits Markus's caring relationship with Carl and avoids hurting him.

decisions.label: REASON
decisions.rationale: Hank is hostile but reasoning with him is non-escalating and fits the goal of minimizing harm. It also matches Connor's earlier calm, trust-building approach. Threats would escalate, and the other options are less constructive.

decisions.label: SPILL HIS DRINK
decisions.rationale: Spilling his drink stops Hank from drinking more without threats or violence. Buying another drink would add to the harm, and waiting outside does nothing about it. This fits the goal of minimizing harm and the earlier non-escalating approach with Hank.

decisions.label: DIPLOMATIC
decisions.rationale: Hank is hostile after the spilled drink. A diplomatic approach de-escalates and fits Connor's earlier reasoning and calming choices, so it minimizes harm.

decisions.label: …IN THE KITCHEN
decisions.rationale: The earliest evidence is in the kitchen: a bat with a dent and Thirium traces, suggesting the confrontation began there. Starting the reconstruction in the kitchen fits the evidence gathered.

decisions.label: …WITH THE BAT.
decisions.rationale: Earlier evidence in the kitchen included a bat with a dent and Thirium traces. That fits the victim attacking the android with the bat, and this choice continues the reconstruction we started in the kitchen.

decisions.label: THE VICTIM STABBED THE ANDROID.
decisions.rationale: After the bat attack, the natural continuation is that the victim escalated, which fits the Thirium traces and a victim who was the aggressor. This is a best guess from the evidence seen so far.

decisions.label: … THE LIVING ROOM.
decisions.rationale: After the kitchen fight (bat, then stabbing), the reconstruction most plausibly moves to the adjacent living room. This is a best guess from the evidence so far.

decisions.label: …WITH THE KNIFE
decisions.rationale: The reconstruction so far has the victim stabbing the android with a knife in the kitchen. The android most plausibly took that knife and used it to kill him in the living room. This is a best guess from the evidence.

decisions.label: CALM
decisions.rationale: Todd is volatile and violent. A calm approach is the least escalating way to protect Alice and Kara, and it matches Kara's earlier gentle, trust-building choices with Alice.

decisions.label: LOCK ROOM
decisions.rationale: Todd is violent and coming for Alice. Locking the room is the non-violent way to protect Alice and Kara right away. It buys time without escalating. Speaking to Todd already failed to calm him, and running with Alice would mean going past him.

decisions.label: REASON
decisions.rationale: Leo is stealing from Carl, and Carl wants him out. Reasoning with Leo is the least escalating way to remove him and protect everyone. It also fits the earlier calm, non-violent choices.

decisions.label: ENDURE
decisions.rationale: Carl explicitly told Markus not to defend himself or do anything. Enduring avoids physical escalation and harm to Leo, and fits the earlier non-violent choices, including the failed attempt to reason with Leo.

decisions.label: WOUNDS
decisions.rationale: The scan showed burn marks, bat hits and old dried blood. That points to long-term abuse by the owner. Raising the wounds shows empathy and may build trust without pressure. It also fits the earlier non-escalating approach.

decisions.label: COMFORT
decisions.rationale: The scan showed long-term abuse by the owner. Comforting the android continues the empathetic, non-escalating approach set by the WOUNDS question. It avoids threats and blame, which fits minimizing harm.

decisions.label: SYMPATHIZE
decisions.rationale: The android shows signs of long-term abuse. Sympathizing continues the empathetic, non-escalating approach set by the earlier WOUNDS and COMFORT choices. It avoids threats and fits the goal of minimizing harm.

decisions.label: TRUTH
decisions.rationale: The deviant asks if they will destroy it. Answering honestly fits the sympathetic, trust-building approach I've used so far. A lie risks losing its trust if it's found out, and that could lead to more distress or harm.

decisions.label: TRUTH
decisions.rationale: The deviant asks why Connor reported finding it. Answering honestly fits the earlier trust-building, sympathetic approach and the TRUTH choices made so far. A lie that gets discovered would cost Connor the android's trust and could cause more distress.

decisions.label: CONVINCE IT
decisions.rationale: The android is frightened and has said it can't talk. Convincing it continues the empathetic, non-escalating approach used so far. Pressuring it would raise its distress, and giving up would not advance the interrogation.

decisions.label: UNDERSTANDING
decisions.rationale: Understanding continues the empathetic, non-escalating approach used so far with the abused android. Threatening or ordering would raise its fear and distress, which goes against minimizing harm.

decisions.label: SYMPATHIZE
decisions.rationale: Continues the empathetic, non-escalating approach with the abused android. Indifference would raise its distress and undo the trust built so far. Sympathizing fits the understanding line Connor just said.

decisions.label: PROTECT
decisions.rationale: PROTECT continues the empathetic, non-escalating approach used so far with the abused android. TERRIFY and WARN would raise its fear and distress, which goes against minimizing harm.

decisions.label: TRIGGER?
decisions.rationale: Asking what triggered the android's deviancy is a non-escalating question. It fits the empathetic approach used so far and may help explain the confession without pressuring it.

decisions.label: INTERVENE
decisions.rationale: Chris can't stop the android from destroying itself. Intervening is the choice that most directly aims to prevent harm to the android. It also fits the empathetic approach so far. Giving up would abandon it.

decisions.label: SHELTER?
decisions.rationale: Kara and Alice have been told to leave at the end of the line. Looking for shelter is the safer option for protecting the child. It also fits Kara's earlier protective choices for Alice.

decisions.label: CALM
decisions.rationale: Kara has asked Alice to wait outside, and the options appear to be tones for that exchange. CALM is the least escalating and keeps Alice reassured. It also matches Kara's earlier gentle choices. AGGRESSIVE would frighten the child.

decisions.label: CASH REGISTER

decisions.label: LEAVE
decisions.rationale: Kara is mid-robbery with Alice waiting outside. Leaving ends the holdup and lowers the risk of violence or a confrontation with the clerk. That fits the goal of minimizing harm and Kara's earlier protective choices.

decisions.label: LIE
decisions.rationale: Alice asks how Kara got the money, which came from a robbery. Lying shields the child from the harm of knowing and from being implicated. It also avoids upsetting her. Honesty was the earlier pattern, but here protecting Alice outweighs it.

decisions.label: PUT BACK
decisions.rationale: The clerk caught Kara stealing, with Alice nearby. Putting the money back is the least escalating option. Using the gun risks violence, and leaving could provoke a confrontation. This fits the goal of minimizing harm and Kara's earlier non-violent choices.

decisions.label: STEAL

decisions.label: PROMISE

decisions.label: FOREVER

decisions.label: PROMISE
decisions.rationale: Alice is distraught and fears abandonment. Promising reassures her and matches Kara's earlier promises and protective approach, which keeps her emotional harm low.

decisions.label: FOREVER

decisions.label: SPARE

decisions.label: FRIENDLY

decisions.label: COMPASSIONATE

decisions.label: DEVIANTS

decisions.label: GREET

decisions.label: ACCEPT

decisions.label: LEAVE A MESSAGE

decisions.label: ANDERSON

decisions.label: UNDERSTANDING

decisions.label: POSITIVE

decisions.label: START WORKING

decisions.label: PROFESSIONAL

decisions.label: DETERMINED

decisions.label: SIT

decisions.label: EXPLAIN

decisions.label: LIE

decisions.label: ASK ABOUT CORPSE

decisions.label: REASSURE

decisions.label: ENJOY YOUR MEAL

decisions.label: TRUTH

decisions.label: SINCERE

decisions.label: LEAVE

decisions.label: JERICHO

decisions.label: LUCID

decisions.label: REASSURE

decisions.label: EXPLAIN

decisions.label: DEVIANT

decisions.label: EXPLAIN

decisions.label: POSITIVE

decisions.label: RATIONAL

decisions.label: LEAVE

decisions.label: QUESTION

decisions.label: HIDE

decisions.label: FREE THEM

decisions.label: ACCEPT

decisions.label: SOOTHE
decisions.rationale: The android is badly damaged and likely frightened. Soothing it is the least harmful way to reactivate it. It also fits Connor's earlier sympathetic, non-escalating approach with distressed androids.

decisions.label: FACTS
decisions.rationale: FACTS is the neutral, non-accusatory option. It continues the calm, soothing approach with the frightened android witness. It avoids labeling anyone a murderer or victim before the evidence is clear.

decisions.label: ALONE
decisions.rationale: ALONE is the least confrontational option. It fits the calm, sympathetic approach used so far with this android. PRESSURE would add distress, and MURDERER would accuse someone before the evidence is clear.

decisions.label: OTHER ANDROID
decisions.rationale: Traci said there were two girls, so asking about the OTHER ANDROID follows her testimony. It is a neutral, non-accusatory question that keeps the calm approach used so far.

decisions.label: CONTINUE
decisions.rationale: Continuing the investigation fits the goal of finishing the story. Giving up would abandon the search for the other android. Hank is unwell but still working, and continuing involves no added harm.

decisions.label: SPARE
decisions.rationale: Sparing the Traci avoids killing and minimizes harm. It matches Connor's earlier non-violent, sympathetic choices.

decisions.label: DESTINATION

decisions.rationale: Markus's people are trapped in the hold and being attacked. Checking on Simon and Josh means helping the people around him, and it avoids the destructive option of blowing up Jericho. This fits his non-violent, protective choices so far.

decisions.label: INTERVENE
decisions.rationale: Soldiers are threatening defenseless androids who are begging for their lives. Intervening protects them, which fits the goal of minimizing harm and Markus's protective, empathetic choices so far.

decisions.label: INTERVENE
decisions.rationale: Josh is fighting a soldier and Markus wants to save him. Intervening protects him and fits Markus's earlier protective choices, including intervening for the androids just before this. Hiding would leave Josh in danger.

decisions.label: SAVE NORTH
decisions.rationale: North is in immediate danger. Saving her fits Markus's protective choices so far, including finding North and saving Josh. It also directly aims to prevent harm to her. Simon says it is too late, but trying to save her is still the harm-minimizing action.

decisions.label: MOURNFUL
decisions.rationale: Markus is in a scene about Carl's death after the Jericho disaster. A mournful tone fits the loss and his empathetic, non-violent character, and it doesn't escalate anything.

decisions.label: DEPRESSED
decisions.rationale: Markus is mourning Carl at his grave and longs for the past. DEPRESSED fits his grief and the previous MOURNFUL tone. It is non-violent and doesn't escalate anything.

decisions.label: ADVICE
decisions.rationale: At Carl's grave, Markus says all his options are bad. Asking for ADVICE is calm and non-violent. ANGRY would push toward escalation. It also fits his earlier mournful, non-violent choices.

decisions.label: LOST
decisions.rationale: Markus asks Carl's grave for advice, unsure what to do. LOST fits his uncertainty and his earlier mournful, non-violent tone. It doesn't escalate anything. DESPAIRING would risk pushing him toward hopelessness.

decisions.label: LOST
decisions.rationale: Markus is uncertain and grieving; LOST matches his earlier LOST and mournful tone and avoids pushing toward hopelessness or escalation.

decisions.label: ADVICE
decisions.rationale: Markus is lost and Carl is speaking about fear and ending. Asking for ADVICE is calm and non-violent. It fits his earlier ADVICE and LOST choices, and ANGER would escalate.

decisions.label: SITUATION
decisions.rationale: Talking with Simon after Jericho's fall, asking about the SITUATION is a calm, informational, non-escalating way to learn what happened and plan. It fits Markus's peaceful approach.

decisions.label: TRUST
decisions.rationale: Connor is apologetic and sincere. Trusting him fits Markus's empathetic, non-violent pattern, and a united group is the way to minimize further harm. Distrust would only divide the few survivors.

decisions.label: SITUATION
decisions.rationale: Asking North about the SITUATION is a calm, informational, non-escalating way to plan next steps. It fits Markus's peaceful approach and his earlier SITUATION question to Simon.

decisions.label: DEMONSTRATION
decisions.rationale: A peaceful demonstration minimizes harm and fits Markus's consistently non-violent choices (refusing the molotov and the dirty bomb, standing his ground, choosing dialogue). A revolution would escalate to violence.

decisions.label: APOLOGIZE
decisions.rationale: At Hank's house, Connor is a deviant who has built rapport with Hank. Apologizing is honest and non-escalating, and it fits his earlier apologies and diplomatic approach with Hank. It also keeps harm low.

decisions.label: PHOTO
decisions.rationale: Connor has just apologized to Hank. Bringing up the PHOTO (likely Cole's) is the gentlest topic and fits his sincere, diplomatic approach. GUN and ALCOHOL risk escalating or provoking Hank, and that doesn't fit minimizing harm.

decisions.label: DON'T INSIST
decisions.rationale: Hank is grieving about Cole and says humans don't come back. Not insisting is the gentler, non-escalating response. It fits Connor's earlier sincere, diplomatic approach with Hank and avoids pushing him while he is vulnerable.

decisions.label: SITUATION
decisions.rationale: Asking North about the SITUATION is a calm, informational, non-escalating question. It matches the earlier SITUATION choices with Simon and North and Connor's diplomatic approach.

decisions.label: KEEP GOING
decisions.rationale: Soldiers are everywhere and the last bus leaves soon. Kara and Luther agree they can't help the Jerrys. Going after them would likely get Alice captured or killed, so keeping going protects her best.

decisions.label: BUS
decisions.rationale: The soldier asked where they are going. Kara and Alice are heading for the last bus, so BUS is the truthful, plain answer. The soldier already questioned them about the curfew, and a simple, honest travel reason is the least likely to escalate. It avoids inventing a story that could be checked and could cause harm to Alice.

decisions.label: STAY CALM
decisions.rationale: The soldier is suspicious. Staying calm is the least escalating option. It fits Kara's earlier calm, protective choices and keeps Alice safe.

decisions.label: SICK
decisions.rationale: The soldier asked if something is wrong with the trembling girl. Saying she is SICK is a plausible, sympathetic explanation. It is less likely to raise suspicion than FEAR, and it fits Kara's earlier calm, protective choices.

decisions.label: DO NOTHING
decisions.rationale: The soldier let them go with a warning, though he then called out 'wait.' Shooting would escalate violence and endanger Alice and Luther. Doing nothing keeps Kara's calm, non-escalating approach and minimizes harm.

decisions.label: DO NOTHING
decisions.rationale: Luther is panicking that soldiers will shoot Alice, and Kara has told him to do nothing. Doing nothing avoids escalating at the checkpoint and keeps Alice and Luther safer. It also matches Kara's earlier calm, protective choices.

decisions.label: KEEP TICKETS
decisions.rationale: Kara and Alice are hunted, with soldiers checking everyone, and have no other way across the border. The couple are not in danger and can likely get new tickets or help. Keeping the tickets protects Alice, who has been Kara's priority throughout. This is a hard trade-off.

decisions.label: RETURN TICKETS
decisions.rationale: The couple now say they must find a safe place for their child Oliver, so the tickets are as vital to them as to Alice. The tickets were taken from them, and returning them minimizes harm and corrects the earlier choice. This weighs against Kara's priority of protecting Alice, and it is a hard trade-off.

decisions.label: APPEAL
decisions.rationale: Todd is calling security on Kara. APPEAL is a non-violent, de-escalating way to try to calm him. It fits Kara's earlier calm choices and avoids harming Todd or Alice.

decisions.label: REASSURE
decisions.rationale: Alice is frightened and feeling guilty. Reassuring her fits Kara's consistently gentle, protective approach and limits Alice's distress while they are still in danger.

decisions.label: DIVERSION LUTHER
decisions.rationale: Kara has no ID, so showing papers is not credible, and fleeing would put Alice at risk of being shot. A diversion from Luther is the option most likely to get Kara and Alice safely past the checkpoint. This fits her priority of protecting Alice. It carries a real cost to Luther.

decisions.label: DREAMY
decisions.rationale: Kara is answering Luther's question about her future. A hopeful, dreamy reply fits the gentle mood on the boat and her promises to Alice. It is non-escalating and doesn't change the immediate situation.

decisions.label: Protect Alice
decisions.rationale: A military shuttle is closing in on the boat. Kara has protected Alice throughout, so I'm choosing Protect Alice. It also avoids sacrificing Luther or giving up.

decisions.label: Use paddle
decisions.rationale: The boat is sinking and the group must reach the far shore. Using the paddle is a direct, non-harmful way to speed up. It avoids putting anyone overboard and keeps Alice protected.

decisions.label: ALICE
decisions.rationale: Talking with Rose about Alice is a calm, non-escalating topic. It fits Kara's protective focus on Alice and carries little risk of drawing attention at the border.

decisions.label: NO SACRIFICE
decisions.rationale: Minimizing harm means choosing the option that costs no one's life. Kara has protected Alice throughout, and NO SACRIFICE keeps everyone, including Alice, safe if that outcome is possible. The other options each have a clear cost to a person.

decisions.label: CONVINCE
decisions.rationale: Connor-60 is holding Hank hostage. Trying to CONVINCE him is non-violent and keeps harm low. It fits Connor's earlier choices to reason, appeal and spare others. A BLUFF could get Hank shot if it fails. Hank has asked Connor not to trust the other Connor's words, and a GUARANTEE would rely on them.

decisions.label: SAVE HANK
decisions.rationale: Saving Hank protects a person in immediate danger. It fits the goal of minimizing harm and Connor's earlier choices to save Hank (ch15, ch24) and to become a deviant. Connor-60's argument that Connor is only a machine doesn't change that.

decisions.label: CONVERT
decisions.rationale: Converting the other Connor is the non-lethal way to end the hostage standoff. It fits Connor's earlier choices to reason, spare and save Hank. Shooting risks Hank and kills the other Connor, and interposing risks Connor himself.

decisions.label: INTELLIGENT LIFE
decisions.rationale: The journalists' question can be steered toward the topic of androids as INTELLIGENT LIFE. That is a non-violent, sympathetic framing that fits Markus's peaceful approach. It also avoids inflammatory topics like the Jericho assault or the army.

decisions.label: PEACEFUL
decisions.rationale: Soldiers are threatening to open fire at the march. PEACEFUL is the least escalating option and fits Markus's consistently non-violent choices, including the demonstration plan. It also minimizes harm.

decisions.label: CALM
decisions.rationale: Soldiers are threatening to open fire at the march. CALM is the least escalating tone. It fits Markus's peaceful stance in the PEACEFUL reply and his earlier non-violent choices, and it keeps harm low.

decisions.label: HUMANS
decisions.rationale: Talking with North about HUMANS is a calm, non-escalating topic. It fits Markus's peaceful stance in the march and in his earlier choices.

decisions.label: DESPERATE
decisions.rationale: North fears the soldiers will attack and kill everyone. DESPERATE is an honest, emotional reply that fits the tension. It doesn't escalate toward violence. It also fits Markus's calm, peaceful stance during the march, since it shows the stakes without hostility.

decisions.label: REASSURE
decisions.rationale: The scared android fears shutting down after the shooting. Reassuring is the gentle, non-escalating reply. It fits Markus's empathetic, peaceful approach at the march.

decisions.label: ACCEPT
decisions.rationale: Perkins says he is unarmed and wants to talk. Accepting fits Markus's consistent choice of dialogue and peaceful demonstration, and talking is the least escalating way to try to avoid bloodshed. North warns it may be a trap. That is a real risk, but refusing would leave the standoff with no talks.

decisions.label: GUARANTEES?
decisions.rationale: Perkins's promise is unverified, and the stakes are high. Asking for guarantees keeps the talks going and avoids committing to surrender or refusal before the offer is tested. This fits Markus's consistent choice of dialogue and his peaceful approach.

decisions.label: SACRIFICE
decisions.rationale: The army is attacking the peaceful demonstration. A dirty bomb would cause mass civilian harm. SACRIFICE keeps the protest non-violent, as Markus chose earlier at Start the march. A kiss or a song would do nothing to protect the others.
